content:
Over the past few days, two reports have pointed to different ways Apple could increase profits by boosting services revenue.

In my view, Apple absolutely should adopt the first approach, but not the second — and it looks like Phil Schiller would agree…

Let me first summarize the two reports.

Home security and monitoring service

On Friday, Bloomberg reported that Apple may be planning to launch a brand-new home security and monitoring service, expected to debut alongside some of the long-awaited new home hardware.

Extracting more revenue from the App Store

A second Bloomberg report on Sunday said Apple is exploring various ways to squeeze more revenue and profit from the App Store.

Apple should not adopt the latter approach

On the contrary, I believe the second approach would be a very serious mistake.

Apple's de facto monopoly over iPhone app sales is already being questioned by regulators around the world. In most countries, if you want to sell an iPhone app, you have to go through the official App Store, with no choice but to accept Apple's terms and zero room to negotiate.

I know many people feel that nobody is forcing you to buy an iPhone or develop apps for it, but that view does not align with how even the most laissez-faire capitalism actually works: even in the US, antitrust law has existed since 1890. Once you reach a certain level of market dominance, you are subject to conduct rules to ensure you do not abuse that position.

Trying to extract more money from the App Store runs counter to the idea of "skating to where the puck is going" — and Schiller reportedly agrees. Bloomberg noted this was one of the reasons he stepped back from frontline work.

Innovative services are the right direction

Apple should launch new, innovative services that customers are happy to pay for. I can easily see the value of Apple offering a home security monitoring service.

I said back in 2024 that developing its own smart home cameras would be one of the smartest moves the company could make. I expressed the same view at the time about the long-rumored Apple smart doorbell. Adding an optional service bundle to security products makes complete sense, for two reasons.

First, all the privacy reasons I mentioned earlier apply. HomeKit Secure Video has already done a great deal of work to protect security camera footage privacy. If there's one company I'd trust to run AI analysis on security camera footage, it's Apple.

Second, Apple is of course best placed to fully integrate security hardware and services within the HomeKit ecosystem. I firmly believe there are many other areas where Apple could offer a similar advantage.

For me, the point is that Apple needs to treat services with the same attitude it applies to hardware — build excellent products that customers are happy and willing to pay for, rather than making money in ways that annoy customers, developers, and regulators.

What do you think? Feel free to share your views in the comments.
